clue.text: Chicken, perhaps rearing a layer

indicators.note: in a down clue, rearing up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a chicken is one example of an animal

explanation.surface: A hen being raised to lay eggs, a layer in the farmyard sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Layer' pretends to be an egg-laying hen; it is the definition, a thin sheet.
explanation.definitionFit: A lamina is a thin plate or sheet, one stratum of a laminated material.

clue.text: Tennis champion almost gets nothing

indicators.note: almost the whole name, so its final letter is cut off

parts.note: Rafael Nadal, the Spanish tennis champion

explanation.surface: A tennis star nearly ends up with no reward at all.
explanation.walkthrough: Rafa Nadal loses his last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Nada is Spanish-derived slang for nothing at all, used in English informally.

clue.text: Paignton turned out to be pathetic

indicators.note: the letters of the place name are turned out, rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A verdict on the Devon seaside resort of Paignton: a sad, pitiful place.
explanation.walkthrough: Paignton is a seaside town in Devon, England; its letters rearranged give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pathetic in its original sense means arousing pity or sadness, which is what poignant means.

clue.text: Go off fish served up for cook

indicators.note: in a down clue, served up means the letters are sent upwards, read in reverse

parts.note: to go off, as food does, is to rot
cod is a fish

explanation.surface: Fish that has spoiled is passed off to a cook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cook' is a verb here, as in cooking the books: falsifying.
explanation.definitionFit: To doctor and to cook both mean to tamper with or falsify something such as accounts.

clue.text: Stunt with tattered shirt, one that Jesus may oppose?

parts.note: an antic is a playful trick or stunt

indicators.note: a tattered shirt is torn apart, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A prank involving a ripped shirt, the sort of thing a religious figure might object to.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is playful: the figure is defined by being Christ's opponent.
explanation.definitionFit: In Christian belief the Antichrist is the great adversary who stands against Christ before the end of the world.

clue.text: Strongman — he's smuggling riches from the south

indicators.note: something smuggled is hidden inside, so one piece is carried within the other

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe dropped

indicators.note: in a down clue, read from the south means from the bottom upwards, so the word is reversed

parts.note: lucre is money or riches, especially ill-gotten

explanation.surface: A strongman sneaks stolen wealth past the border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Filthy lucre' is the idiom for riches.
explanation.definitionFit: Hercules is the mythological hero famed for his immense strength and twelve labours.

clue.text: Afraid no air's circulating in home

indicators.note: the rearranged letters sit inside the word for home

parts.note: a pad is slang for one's home or flat

indicators.note: the letters move round, as air circulates, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone stuck in a stuffy house panics that there is no fresh air.
explanation.definitionFit: Paranoid loosely means fearful and suspicious of others, so afraid is a fair synonym.

clue.text: Read about Moriarty, void of imagination

indicators.note: about here means moving around, so the letters are scrambled
void means emptied, so only the first and last letters of the name remain

explanation.surface: A critic reads up on Sherlock Holmes's nemesis and finds the books unimaginative.
explanation.walkthrough: Moriarty is Professor Moriarty, Sherlock Holmes's arch-enemy; emptying him leaves MY.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreamy describes something belonging to fancy or reverie rather than reality, the realm of imagination.

clue.text: Old relative's ignoring large cats

indicators.note: ignoring the letter for large means it is left out

parts.note: relative's read as relatives, uncles
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: An elderly relative takes no notice of big cats.
explanation.walkthrough: The ounce is another name for the snow leopard.
explanation.definitionFit: The ounce, or snow leopard, is a large wild cat of the Central Asian mountains.

clue.text: Letters picked up with a permit

indicators.note: picked up means heard, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: V's, the plural of the letter V, written vees

explanation.surface: Correspondence arrives together with a travel authorisation.
explanation.walkthrough: Several letter V's, vees, are said aloud to give VIS, then A follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A visa is an official endorsement in a passport allowing entry to a country, a kind of permit.

clue.text: Area covered by remarkably energetic family member

indicators.note: the single letter is covered, enclosed, by the rearranged letters
remarkably suggests something out of the ordinary, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A lively relative spreads herself across the whole room.
explanation.definitionFit: A great-niece is the granddaughter of one's sibling, a relation in the extended family.

clue.text: Fellow traveller on vacation in front of a sacred text

parts.note: a fellow is a man

indicators.note: the word is vacated, emptied of its middle, leaving its outer letters

explanation.surface: A man on holiday stands before a holy scripture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In front of' just places the pieces in order.
explanation.definitionFit: A mantra is a word or verse from Hindu or Buddhist scripture chanted as a sacred formula.

clue.text: Has a go at drinking a beer, developed as a source of wintergreen

indicators.note: drinking takes something inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: to have a go at something is to try it, so tries

indicators.note: developed means changed and worked up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone sampling a newly brewed beer flavoured with wintergreen.
explanation.definitionFit: The teaberry is the American shrub Gaultheria procumbens, whose leaves yield oil of wintergreen.

clue.text: Orders Dutch artist to pursue damages

indicators.note: the artist pursues, comes after, the word for damages

parts.note: mars means spoils or damages
Frans Hals, the Dutch Golden Age portrait painter

explanation.surface: A Dutch painter is told to chase compensation through the courts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Damages' looks like a legal noun but is a verb; 'Orders' is also a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To marshal is to arrange or put in order, as troops or arguments are marshalled.

clue.text: Where a piglet may be taken to get warm

parts.note: taken to a place, so the directional word that goes before a destination
a piglet is kept in a pigpen, which 'Where' marks as its place

explanation.surface: A farmer brings a piglet into its pen to keep it cosy.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole phrase describes a journey to the pig's home; read as plain words it spells the answer, while 'to get' links it to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Toasty is an informal word for comfortably heated, cosy and pleasantly warm.

clue.text: Young man brewing green tea

indicators.note: brewing stirs things up, so the letters are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: A youth making himself a cup of green tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A teenager is a youth aged thirteen to nineteen, so a young man fits.

clue.text: Aristotle finally caught in this moral framework

indicators.note: finally means the last letter of the philosopher's name
the abbreviation sits inside the word this

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: Aristotle at last finds himself caught up in this system of morals.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, Aristotle wrote the Nicomachean Ethics.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethics is the system of moral principles that governs behaviour, a moral framework.

clue.text: Time left for supporting cast to discover Arthurian site

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting pieces sit underneath, after the word they support

parts.note: a cast is a tint, a slight shade of colour
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Theatre talk: time is set aside for the supporting cast to find a legendary location.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporting cast' reads as the minor actors, but 'cast' is a colour shade and 'supporting' places the other pieces below it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tintagel in Cornwall is the castle legend names as King Arthur's birthplace.

clue.text: Good-for-nothing fruit farm

indicators.note: for means in place of, so one letter replaces the other

parts.note: an orange is a fruit
O, the round figure zero, means nothing

explanation.surface: A lazy layabout runs an orchard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good-for-nothing' reads as a layabout, but it is an instruction: G in place of O.
explanation.definitionFit: A grange is a country house with farm buildings, a farmstead.

clue.text: Ceremonial guard releasing female bird

indicators.note: releasing lets the letter go, so it is dropped

parts.note: Beefeaters are the Yeoman Warders who guard the Tower of London in ceremonial dress

explanation.surface: A Tower of London guard lets a woman go free.
explanation.walkthrough: Beefeaters are the uniformed warders at the Tower of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The bee-eater is a brightly coloured bird that catches bees and other insects in flight.

clue.text: Eastender's hat refurbishment takes time, on reflection

indicators.note: a reflection is a mirror image, so the result is read backwards
the word takes in the letter, holding it inside

parts.note: a refit is a refurbishment

explanation.surface: A Londoner's hat restoration takes a while, when one thinks about it.
explanation.walkthrough: An Eastender is a Londoner from the East End, home of Cockney rhyming slang: titfer is short for tit-for-tat, rhyming with hat.
explanation.definitionFit: Titfer is Cockney rhyming slang for a hat, from tit-for-tat.

clue.text: Bottom two numbers

parts.note: the first of the two numbers: N, the algebraic symbol for an unspecified number
the second number, read as a numb-er, something that numbs: an anaesthetic gas

explanation.surface: A curt instruction about the last two figures in a list.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'numbers' as things that make you numb: ether is an old anaesthetic. N is the maths letter for any number.
explanation.definitionFit: Nether means lower or underneath, so it fits bottom used as an adjective.

clue.text: I'm not sure a sailor lies about mistakes

parts.note: er is the hesitant noise of someone unsure

indicators.note: something that lies about is turned round, so these letters are read backwards

parts.note: tar is an old word for a sailor

explanation.surface: A doubtful speaker accuses a seaman of telling untruths about errors.
explanation.definitionFit: Errata is the Latin plural for errors, especially printing errors listed in a book.

clue.text: Muse about Italian following mother country

indicators.note: the Muse's piece follows, comes after, the word for mother

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother

indicators.note: the Muse's name goes about, around, the abbreviation

parts.note: Urania is the Muse of astronomy

explanation.surface: A poet broods on an Italian, then on his mother's homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Muse' looks like a verb, ponder, but it is one of the nine Muses.
explanation.definitionFit: Mauritania is a nation in north-west Africa on the Atlantic coast.

clue.text: Blunt end of skewer stuck into piece of meat

indicators.note: the letter is stuck into, placed inside, the other word

parts.note: a cut is a piece of meat from a butcher

indicators.note: the end of the word means its last letter

explanation.surface: The blunt tip of a kebab skewer is pushed into a joint of meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blunt' looks like it describes the skewer's end but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Curt and blunt both describe speech that is short, brusque and rudely direct.

clue.text: Wine in Bordeaux, it's OK

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ..., the Spanish sparkling wine
second meaning: French ça va, it's fine, as one would say in Bordeaux

explanation.walkthrough: Bordeaux suggests French wine, but the wine is Spanish; Bordeaux just signals French speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Cava is a Spanish sparkling wine, while the French phrase ça va means all is well.

clue.text: Divorce wife ultimately finds difficult

parts.note: to sever is to cut off or divorce

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Splitting up with one's wife turns out to be hard.
explanation.definitionFit: Severe can mean hard to endure or deal with, as in a severe test.

clue.text: Drifting, veteran explorer's beginning to weaken

indicators.note: drifting letters wander out of order, so they are rearranged
the beginning of the word means its first letter

explanation.surface: An old explorer, drifting off course, starts to lose his strength.
explanation.definitionFit: To enervate is to drain of energy or vitality, making someone feeble.
